<reason>Both sides built serious, well-structured cases and the debate stayed tightly on the motion. CON's core strategy — defining "real" consent as already requiring information, competence, and freedom from other-party coercion, and then relocating every apparent counterexample's wrongness into "background conditions" or "third parties" — was intellectually disciplined and produced the sharpest single exchange of the debate: the commerce-condemning reductio against PRO's gambler example (lottery tickets and desserts also exploit known bias). PRO never fully closed that gap, and CON's Pressure Questions exposed it well. But PRO's meta-level rebuttal landed harder over the course of the debate: if consent is only "valid" once it satisfies fairness-adjacent conditions like adequate information and absence of manipulation, then consent was never doing the moral work alone — which is PRO's exact thesis, not a refutation of it. CON's fallback move of admitting that transactions like desperate sweatshop labor or kidney sales *are* consensual but that any wrong lies purely in "background conditions" is a costly bite of the bullet that PRO exploited effectively in the closing, and CON's "name the wronged party or admit it's just sensibility" demand imported a policy/tort standard into an ethics question, which PRO correctly flagged as a category error. PRO's throughline (the gap between "they agreed" and "this was fine") was clearer and more consistently pressed across rounds, giving PRO the marginally stronger path to the vote, though the debate was close and both sides executed well within a genuinely live clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over the derivatives-buyer/gambler example — CON's reductio that all commerce exploits known psychological bias (lottery tickets, desserts) versus PRO's attempted "wanted value vs. manufactured error" distinction — was the most decisive clash, exposing real weakness in PRO's cleanest example while also showing CON's framework can only condemn wrongs by relocating them outside the transaction.</best_rebuttal>
